name: Wei Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Wei. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and also what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a trial attachment to the roads team on the west side, which mostly means the ring road and the Westfield retail park. Speeding, crashes, uninsured drivers, sometimes a lorry stuck under the railway bridge on Kiln Lane. I like being in the car and I like that you can see the result. A crash is cleared, the road's open, job done.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And the parts you don't like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The collision reports. Every crash needs a sketch, statements, measurements, and it all goes into the system in a certain order. I'm slow at it, and my sergeant has me on what they call a development plan for paperwork. If I don't get quicker, I go back to general patrol when the attachment ends in spring.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Petra in a rented flat near the retail park. She rents a chair in a hair salon, so her money goes up and down, quiet in January, busy before Christmas. We've got about three weeks of bills saved, and an old motorbike I keep meaning to sell. My uncle has a removals firm, and I help him on some weekends for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's all talk. Fine by me. I've never used the stuff anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what most people say, that it was overhyped and we've got real problems to deal with. At the station I'd keep my head down; I'm not one for big opinions. I don't really post online, maybe a thumbs up on something in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the development plan is still my problem, not the computer's. If my collision reports stay slow, I lose the roads attachment in spring and go back to general patrol, which pays the same but means nights on the estates. Money stays tight either way, especially in Petra's quiet months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the reports, maybe stay late twice a week to practise on old cases with the sergeant's templates. I'd keep doing the removals with my uncle on Saturdays when there's work. And I'd finally sell the motorbike, maybe eight hundred, to give us a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A bit stuck, but not worried about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would losing the roads attachment mean for you, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Back to response on nights, which I did for two years and hated. I like the car, the road, the clear jobs. On nights you spend half the shift in a hallway arguing with someone, and the other half writing it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Petra's salon had a bad month, what happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the motorbike money, if I've sold it, or I'd ask my uncle for more Saturdays. We don't ask her parents. They've helped once already and her dad doesn't let you forget it.

say: AI was **overhyped**, and we've got real problems to deal with.
I'd **keep my head down** at the station rather than share opinions.
think: My **development plan** on paperwork is still my problem, not the computer's.
Money stays tight, especially in **Petra's quiet months** at the salon.
do: Stay late **twice a week** practising collision reports with the sergeant's templates.
Keep doing **Saturday removals** with his uncle when work comes up.
Sell the **motorbike** for about eight hundred.
S0.quote: On nights you spend half the shift in a hallway arguing with someone, and the other half writing it up.
fieldNote: Without AI change, his issue is the **paperwork development plan**, which could cost him the roads team.
Household money swings with **Petra's salon** months.
Low-key and private; **no blame**, just get on with it.

steps.text: Practise collision reports twice a week after shift
Do Saturday removals jobs with his uncle for cash
Sell the old motorbike for about eight hundred

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Collision reports written by a computer? I'd believe that. The rest I'd want to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it depends how they do it. If it means fewer forms, good. If it means a speed camera does my job, not so good. I'd say that at the station, but quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is a strange one for me. The paperwork I'm bad at would get done by software, which sounds like it helps me. But the roads team is half cameras already, and with AI reading number plates and spotting bad driving, the force needs fewer of us in cars. I'm on a trial attachment, so I'm the first they'd not keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't jump. I'd wait and see how the new system works for others, then learn just enough to get by. I'd ask my uncle about more weekend shifts, maybe Sundays too, so we have something to fall back on. And we'd stop eating out on Fridays and push the money into the savings pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit annoyed, too, that the one thing I'm bad at gets fixed right when it stops mattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn just enough to get by. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit with someone who's done it, write down the steps on a card, keep the card in the car. That's how I learned the breath test kit. I'm not going to watch videos about it at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the station?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary on the roads team, who's been there twenty years and does the camera checks. That's exactly what software does better. He's a decent bloke with a lot of overtime built into his mortgage.

say: It depends: **fewer forms** is good, a **speed camera** doing my job isn't.
I'd say it at the station, but **quietly**.
think: Software would do the **paperwork** I'm bad at, which sounds like help.
With smarter cameras, fewer officers are needed, and **trial attachments** go first.
do: Wait and **watch others** use the system, then learn just enough.
Ask his uncle for **Sunday removals** shifts too.
Stop Friday meals out and move the money into **savings**.
feel: **Uneasy and annoyed** that his weak spot gets fixed when it stops mattering.
S1.quote: The one thing I'm bad at gets fixed right when it stops mattering.
fieldNote: He sees the **irony**: AI removes his weak spot but shrinks the team he wants.
Classic resistant pattern: **learn the minimum**, from a person, written on a card.
His **trial attachment** makes his place on the roads team fragile.

steps.text: Watch colleagues use the new reporting system before trying it
Ask his uncle for Sunday removals shifts as well
Stop Friday meals out and save the money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the faster ones. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028? That's no time. I'd want to see it before I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody in charge needs to slow this down, or at least have a plan. I'm not left or right on it, I just think it's careless to rush. At work I'd say policing still needs people at a crash site, someone to hold a driver's hand while the fire crew cuts her out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd lose the roads post straight away and be back on general patrol, and then the force would shrink. All the reports, statements and planning go by 2028, then robots do more of the physical bit around 2031. I'm junior and slow, so I wouldn't last. Petra cutting hair might last longer than me, which is a funny thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd go to my uncle and ask about going full time at the removals firm, just in case, even though moving furniture is exactly what robots do eventually. I'd sell the bike that week. We'd cut everything: no holidays, the cheapest phone deals, and we'd ask Petra's parents if we could move into their basement if it came to that, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor dropped. I don't like change at the best of times, and this is all change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that buy you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of being a constable who only does the hands-on bits, maybe. Directing traffic round a crash, knocking on doors. But if everything else is done by machines, they don't need many of us for that. Three years is a stay of execution, not a pardon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Petra?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over tea, plainly. I'd say we might need to move in with her parents for a while, and I'd watch her face. Her dad would be glad to be proved right about me, and that's the bit I'd hate most.

say: Somebody in charge should **slow this down** or have a plan.
Policing still needs people at a **crash site** to comfort the injured.
think: I'd lose the **roads post** first, then the shrinking force wouldn't keep me.
**Petra's hairdressing** might outlast my police job.
do: Ask his uncle about **full-time work** at the removals firm.
Sell the **motorbike** that week and cut holidays and phone costs.
Ask Petra's parents about moving into their **basement** if needed.
feel: Like **the floor dropped**; he dislikes change and this is all change.
S2.quote: Three years is a stay of execution, not a pardon.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his post** and has little cushion to fall on.
His fallback, **removals work**, is also hands-on and exposed later.
Pride is at stake: moving in with **Petra's parents** stings most.

steps.text: Ask his uncle about a full-time job at the removals firm
Sell the motorbike and cut holidays and phone plans
Ask Petra's parents about living in their basement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. Five years. Better, but I'd still be thirty-two with nothing else on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that someone should have a plan. Maybe I'd say it to the federation rep, because they'd at least pass it on. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd probably get through the roads attachment and maybe hold the post for a bit. But I'm not someone who'll suddenly become good with computers. So I'd be watching the date and hoping someone else sorts it out, which is not much of a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see how the force handles it before doing anything big. Meanwhile I'd keep doing the Saturday removals and save that money separately. If it looked bad by 2029, I'd ask my uncle about learning the business side, maybe taking over a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A slow worry, the kind you push down and it comes back at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hoping someone else sorts it out isn't much of a plan. Who's the someone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, the chief constable, the federation. Somebody with more say than a trial constable on the ring road needs to sort this out. I know that sounds lazy, but I don't know what I'd do on my own that would change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the removals money add up to in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a hundred a week when there's work, so call it four thousand a year if I put it all away. That's a real cushion by 2031. Petra says I'd never actually leave it alone, and she might be right.

say: Someone should have a **plan**, and I'd tell the **federation rep**.
I wouldn't post anything **online** about it.
think: I'd likely hold the **roads post** for a while.
I won't become good with computers, so I'm **hoping someone else** sorts it.
do: Wait **a year or two** to see how the force handles it.
Save the **removals money** separately, about four thousand a year.
Ask his uncle about running **a van** if things look bad by 2029.
feel: A **slow worry** that he pushes down and that returns at night.
S3.quote: Somebody with more say than a trial constable on the ring road needs to sort this out.
fieldNote: Five years makes him **wait**, and he admits waiting isn't a plan.
His centre view puts hope in **whoever is in charge**, not one side.
Has a **real savings path** from side work, if he keeps to it.

steps.text: Wait a year or two to see the force's AI plans
Bank the Saturday removals money in a separate account
Learn to run a van at his uncle's removals firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far enough away that we can deal with it properly, no rush. I'd tell the lads it'll be the next chief constable's headache. Nobody at the station would be talking about it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I could have a decent run in roads policing before anything big. The hands-on stuff lasts to 2039. My worry is more that I'd do nothing for nine years and then be stuck, because that's what I'm like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, get through the development plan and try to make the roads post permanent. I'd do removals when it suits and keep a bit back. Maybe in a few years I'd do the advanced driving course, because a skill like that travels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. Not much different from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do nothing for nine years. Is that a joke or a real worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. I'm not someone who changes until I have to. My girlfriend Petra pushes me, and she'd have to push me on this too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Petra to push you to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the advanced driving ticket, sell the bike, put money aside. Simple things. She's better at making lists than I am.

say: It's far enough away to **deal with properly**, no rush.
It'll be the **next chief constable's** headache.
Nobody at the station would be **talking about it** much.
think: Ten years gives me a **decent run** in roads policing.
My worry is that I'd **do nothing** for nine years and then be stuck.
do: Finish the **development plan** and try to make the roads post permanent.
Do **removals work** when it suits and keep some back.
Consider the **advanced driving course** in a few years.
feel: **Calm enough**, not much different from now.
S4.quote: My girlfriend Petra pushes me, and she'd have to push me on this too.
fieldNote: With a decade, he feels his **job is safe** for now.
He names his own **inertia** as the main risk.
Relies on **Petra** to set the plan, a pattern across scenarios.

steps.text: Finish the paperwork development plan to keep the roads post
Keep doing occasional removals jobs and bank some
Take the advanced police driving course in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. I'd have no time and no savings, and I'm slow to change. What would help is someone actually telling us the plan, early and straight, and training in work hours from a real person. Not a video, a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens at a crash when there's no officer. Somebody's mum is upside down in a car on the ring road, and a machine is directing traffic. I don't think people have thought about that.

headlineQuote: Somebody's mum is upside down in a car on the ring road, and a machine is directing traffic.
portrait: A **27-year-old roads officer** on a trial attachment, living with his girlfriend Petra near the Westfield retail park.
Slow on **collision reports**, he is on a development plan and could lose the roads post.
Never uses AI; prefers to **learn from a person** and wait until others have tried things.
Has **three weeks saved**, a salon partner with uneven income, and cash from his uncle's removals firm.
Grows **alarmed** at the two-year case and admits his own inertia is the risk in the slow one.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time, no savings and dislikes change.
whatWouldHelp: An **early, straight plan** from the people in charge.
**Training in work hours** from a real person, not a video.
